entries.title: CPU %
entries.technical: Percent of CPU time spent non-idle, sampled every 5 s by gopsutil and exposed as cpu_pct in metrics.Snapshot. Source: internal/metrics/system.go.
entries.plain: How busy your Pi has been recently. 100% means the CPU is fully loaded; sustained high values can make the dashboard feel sluggish.

entries.title: RAM %
entries.technical: Percent of physical memory in use, exposed as ram_pct. Excludes swap. Pressure rises when active working set approaches the Pi's installed RAM.
entries.plain: How much of your Pi's memory is in use. Above 90% means the Pi is close to swapping or killing processes.

entries.title: Swap %
entries.technical: Percent of swap space in use, exposed as swap_pct. Sustained non-zero swap on a Pi indicates memory pressure that the kernel is paging to disk.
entries.plain: How much temporary disk space your Pi is using as extra memory. Any sustained swap usage usually means RAM is full.

entries.title: Temperature (°C)
entries.technical: CPU temperature in Celsius, read from /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp on Linux ARM. Exposed as temp_c.
entries.plain: How hot your Pi's chip is right now. Higher than 80°C means the CPU may slow itself down to cool off.

entries.title: Disk usage (root /)
entries.technical: Percent of the root filesystem in use, exposed as disk_pct["/"]. Computed by gopsutil over the / mountpoint.
entries.plain: How full the Pi's main disk is. When this approaches 100% the system can't write logs, backups, or new files.

entries.title: Load average
entries.technical: Linux 1/5/15-minute load average via sysinfo. Roughly 'how many processes are wanting CPU'. Reference value: load equal to the number of cores is full utilisation.
entries.plain: How many things your Pi is trying to do at once. If this stays higher than the number of CPU cores, your Pi is overloaded.

entries.title: Gateway probe
entries.technical: ICMP ping every 5 s to the LAN gateway resolved from /proc/net/route. Status is one of ok | unknown | down. Exposed via the wan_gateway_ok variable.
entries.plain: Whether your Pi can reach your home router. If this is down, the Pi is cut off from the local network.

entries.title: Cloudflare probe (1.1.1.1)
entries.technical: ICMP ping every 5 s to 1.1.1.1 — Cloudflare's public DNS resolver. Used as the public-internet reference. Status mirrors the wan_cloudflare_ok variable.
entries.plain: Whether your Pi can reach the public internet. If the gateway is up but this is down, the problem is upstream of your router.

entries.title: DNS probe
entries.technical: DNS query every 5 s for cloudflare.com via 1.1.1.1. Status is ok | unknown | down. Independent of the ICMP gateway/cloudflare probes — DNS can fail even when ping succeeds.
entries.plain: Whether your Pi can look up names like 'github.com'. If ping works but this fails, you have a DNS problem.

entries.title: WAN state machine
entries.technical: Three-state monitor that observes every gateway/cloudflare/DNS probe and emits wan_up / wan_down events. Requires three consecutive failures to declare WAN_DOWN, three successes to recover.
entries.plain: The Pi's overall verdict on whether your home internet is up. Smooths over single missed pings so a flaky cable doesn't trigger a false alarm.

entries.title: Probe RTT (ms)
entries.technical: Round-trip time of the most recent successful ICMP probe in milliseconds. NetSample.RTTMs is persisted for the network history chart.
entries.plain: How long a 'are you there?' message takes to come back. Higher numbers mean a slower or congested link.

entries.title: Packet loss %
entries.technical: Percent of probes within a window whose Status != ok. Used by the sustained_packet_loss insight rule. Variable: loss_pct.
entries.plain: How many of the last few 'are you there?' messages got no answer. Above a few percent over time means a degraded link.

entries.title: Jitter (ms)
entries.technical: Standard deviation of probe RTT over a short window. High jitter degrades real-time traffic (VoIP, video calls) even if average latency is fine.
entries.plain: How much the response time bounces around. Steady is good; spiky means video calls and game traffic will stutter.

entries.title: Offline LAN devices
entries.technical: Count of LAN devices currently in state=offline as observed by the LAN devices orchestrator. Variable: lan_device_offline_count.
entries.plain: How many devices on your home network the Pi can't reach right now. A small number is normal (devices come and go); a sudden burst can mean a wider problem.

entries.title: Systemd service: active
entries.technical: ActiveState='active' from the systemd D-Bus interface — the unit started successfully and its main process is running.
entries.plain: The service is running normally.

entries.title: Systemd service: failed
entries.technical: ActiveState='failed' — the unit terminated with a non-zero exit and exhausted its Restart= policy. Will not run again without intervention.
entries.plain: The service crashed and is not running anymore. Click into Services to inspect logs and restart manually.

entries.title: Systemd service: restarting
entries.technical: ActiveState='activating' or 'reloading' transitionally observed during a Restart= cycle. Sustained restart loops are surfaced by the insights-engine.
entries.plain: The service is in the middle of restarting. If it stays in this state, it's stuck in a crash loop.

entries.title: Docker container: healthy
entries.technical: Docker State.Health.Status='healthy' (or no healthcheck configured and State.Status='running'). Reported via the Docker daemon socket.
entries.plain: The container is running and (if it has a health check) reporting itself as fine.

entries.title: Docker container: unhealthy
entries.technical: Docker State.Health.Status='unhealthy' — the configured healthcheck command has exited non-zero N consecutive times.
entries.plain: The container is running, but its self-check is failing. Something inside the container is broken even though Docker itself didn't kill it.

entries.title: Docker container: restarting
entries.technical: Docker State.Status='restarting' — the daemon is in the middle of bringing the container back up under its restart policy. Sustained restart loops are surfaced as a verdict.
entries.plain: The container keeps crashing and Docker keeps restarting it. Inspect its logs to find the underlying error.

entries.title: Tailscale peer: online
entries.technical: Peer reachable through the Tailscale mesh — Online=true from `tailscale status --json`. Either via direct path or DERP relay.
entries.plain: The other device on your Tailscale network is reachable right now.

entries.title: Tailscale peer: offline
entries.technical: Peer Online=false — Tailscale has not received recent keepalives. The peer device may be powered off, asleep, or have lost internet.
entries.plain: The other device on your Tailscale network can't be reached right now.

entries.title: Tailscale DERP relay
entries.technical: Fallback relay used when no direct path between peers can be negotiated. Slower and uses Tailscale's servers as middlemen.
entries.plain: Your Pi is reaching the other Tailscale device through a relay server, not directly. Still works, just slower.

entries.title: Thermal throttling probable
entries.technical: Triggered by the bundled rule 'thermal-throttling' when temp_c sustains above 80 °C. Source: internal/insights/rules/bundled.json. The CPU is reducing its clock to stay within thermal limits.
entries.plain: Your Pi got too hot and is slowing itself down to cool off. Improve airflow, add a heatsink/fan, or move the Pi out of direct sunlight.

entries.title: CPU saturation
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'cpu-saturation' — sustained cpu_pct above its threshold for several consecutive ticks. Indicates a process is monopolising the CPU.
entries.plain: Something on your Pi is using almost all of the CPU. Check the dashboard for the busiest process.

entries.title: Memory pressure
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'memory-pressure' — ram_pct sustained high, often combined with rising swap_pct. The OS is paging to disk to keep up.
entries.plain: Your Pi is running out of memory. Apps will feel slow because the Pi is shuffling memory to disk.

entries.title: Disk space critical
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'disk-critical' — disk_pct['/'] above 95%. At this point new file writes (logs, backups) start failing.
entries.plain: Your Pi's disk is almost full. Free up space soon or things will start breaking.

entries.title: Service failed
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'service-failed' — at least one tracked systemd unit is in ActiveState='failed' and not auto-restarting. Variable: services_failed.
entries.plain: An important background service crashed. Open the Services page to inspect and restart it.

entries.title: Container failed
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'container-failed' — one or more Docker containers are in unhealthy or restart-loop state. Variable: containers_failed.
entries.plain: A container is unhealthy or stuck in a restart loop. Open Docker to see which one and check its logs.

entries.title: WAN down
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'wan-down' — the WAN state machine has declared WAN_DOWN (three consecutive cloudflare-probe failures). Variable: wan_cloudflare_ok=false.
entries.plain: Your home internet is down — your Pi can't reach the public internet, even though it can reach the local router.

entries.title: Gateway unreachable
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'gateway-unreachable' — wan_gateway_ok=false. The Pi can't even reach its own router.
entries.plain: Your Pi can't talk to your home router. Check the network cable, Wi-Fi connection, or router.

entries.title: Sustained packet loss
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'sustained-packet-loss' — loss_pct above the threshold over a window. The link is up but lossy.
entries.plain: Your internet is up but degraded — calls and video will stutter. Often a Wi-Fi or upstream-ISP issue.

entries.title: LAN offline burst
entries.technical: Bundled rule 'lan-offline-burst' — lan_device_offline_count spiked above the threshold. Often caused by an AP reboot or DHCP outage.
entries.plain: Several devices on your home network went offline at once. Usually an issue with the Wi-Fi access point or router rather than each device.
